meta.title: Who really said "Justification is the article by which the church stands and falls"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Luther's words. The Latin formula comes from later Lutheran theology (Balthasar Meisner, 1615) and condenses a looser line from Luther's Psalm 130 lectures.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Justification is the article by which the church stands and falls'?
meta.ogDescription: Luther never wrote this exact line. It is a later Lutheran formula, first found in Balthasar Meisner (1615), that sums up a looser sentence from Luther's Psalm 130 lectures.

answer.label: Not Martin Luther — a later Lutheran formula
answer.sourceLine: The exact formula, Iustificatio est articulus stantis et cadentis ecclesiae, is first reported in Meisner’s Anthropologia sacra (Wittenberg, 1615), where he presents it as “a proverb of Luther.” The idea is Luther’s, but his own sentence in his Psalm 130 lectures is looser: “if this article stands, the church stands; if it collapses, the church collapses” (Wittenberg Center ↗).

source.heading: Where the formula actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Wittenberg: Johannes Gormannus, 1615. The Heidelblog could confirm the phrase only in the 1663 Wittenberg printing.

source.excerpt: Iustificatio est articulus stantis et cadentis ecclesiae.
trail: The Wittenberg Center says the phrase “cannot be found in Luther’s works.” Drawing on Theodor Mahlmann’s 2003 study, it traces an adaptation to Simon Pauli around 1570 and the wording still in use to Balthasar Meisner in 1615. Mahlmann presents his findings as an interim result (Wittenberg Center ↗).

Justin Taylor of The Gospel Coalition finds no record of Luther using the exact phrase. He cites WA 40/3.352.3 as the closest wording, and Meisner’s Anthropôlogia sacra (1615), which calls it a “proverb of Luther,” as the first use of the exact phrase (The Gospel Coalition, 2011 ↗).

The Heidelblog adds the Reformed theologian Johann Heinrich Alsted (1618, p. 711): “Articulus iustificationis dicitur articulus stantis et cadentis ecclesiae.” It rejects F. Loofs’s suggestion that Valentin Ernst Löscher was the first to use it (Heidelblog ↗).

A scholarly article quotes Luther’s Latin from D. Martin Luthers Werke, vol. 40/3 (Weimar, 1930), p. 352, “in a commentary on Ps. 130, 4.” The volume lists the lectures on the Psalms of Ascent under 1532 (CyberLeninka ↗).
source.excerptNote: In English, “Justification is the article of the church’s standing and falling.” Meisner introduces it as a saying of Luther. Luther’s actual words, in his lecture on Psalm 130:4, are “quia isto articulo stante stat Ecclesia, ruente ruit Ecclesia” (WA 40/3, p. 352). The Wittenberg Center quotes the printed text at WA 40/3:351,34–35 as “Stante enim hac doctrina stat Ecclesia, ruente autem ruit ipsa quoque.”

source.rightsNote: The Latin sources are centuries old: Luther’s 1532 lectures, Meisner’s formula (reported for 1615) and Alsted’s of 1618. The English sentence shown, however, is an anonymous rendering that no single identifiable translation can be credited with, so we assert no copyright status for that exact wording.

author.name: Balthasar Meisner
author.heading: About Balthasar Meisner
author.bio: Balthasar Meisner was born in Dresden in 1587 and died in Wittenberg in 1626. He held the professorship of ethics there and later a chair in theology, and he was a leading voice of Lutheran orthodoxy. His disputations on human nature, the Anthropologia sacra, contain the earliest use researchers have reported of the exact Latin formula calling justification the article of the church’s standing and falling. He credited the saying to Luther.

cite.sourceCitation: Balthasar Meisner, Anthropologia sacra, disputation 24 (Wittenberg: Johannes Gormannus, 1615), as reported in Justin Taylor, “Luther’s Saying: ‘Justification Is the Article by Which the Church Stands and Falls,’” The Gospel Coalition, August 31, 2011. Luther’s nearest wording is in D. Martin Luthers Werke, vol. 40/3 (Weimar, 1930), 352.

misattribution.heading: How Luther got the credit
misattribution.intro: The line is everywhere in textbooks and sermons as a Luther quotation. Luther did hold the view, but the polished formula came from his successors, and one of them put Luther’s name on it.

items.why: Luther’s nearest sentence, in his lecture on Psalm 130:4, is “quia isto articulo stante stat Ecclesia, ruente ruit Ecclesia” (WA 40/3.352.3). Taylor calls the famous version a summary or paraphrase of that sentence, not a direct quotation (The Gospel Coalition, 2018 ↗).

F. Loofs suggested that Löscher first used the phrase, in eighteenth-century polemic against the Pietists. The Heidelblog calls that “clearly incorrect,” since Alsted already used it in 1618 (Heidelblog ↗).

Alsted wrote in 1618 that the article of justification “dicitur” (“is said to be”) the article of the church’s standing and falling. That wording shows the phrase was already circulating, so he was not coining it (The Gospel Coalition ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The formula belongs to post-Reformation Lutheranism. Simon Pauli adapted Luther’s thought around 1570, and Balthasar Meisner fixed the wording in 1615, calling it Luther’s proverb (Wittenberg Center ↗).

context.heading: Why the line stuck to Luther
lead: The slogan is a fair summary of what Luther believed, which is why it attached to him so easily. In the Smalcald Articles he wrote of justification by faith that “of this article nothing can be yielded or surrendered” and that “upon this article all things depend which we teach and practice in opposition to the Pope, the devil, and the [whole] world” (Book of Concord ↗).

His successors condensed that conviction into a Latin tag that was easy to remember. Because Meisner presented it as Luther’s own proverb, the attribution was there from the start, and the tag went on to serve both Lutheran and Reformed theologians.
context.pull: “Stante enim hac doctrina stat Ecclesia, ruente autem ruit ipsa quoque.” — Luther, on Psalm 130:4
